title: Analytical and fitting formulae for solutions to Lyman-alpha radiative transfer equations: the effects of geometry, recoil, and velocity gradients
comment: 19 pages, 9 figures, accepted by MNRAS
summary: Lyman-alpha (Ly$α$) radiative transfer (RT) is important in many astrophysical environments and governed by multiple physical processes. In this paper, we provide analytical formulae/procedures for the solutions to Ly$α$ RT equations under three simple geometrical symmetries and investigate the effects of atomic recoil and gas bulk motion. We first study Ly$α$ spectra by solving Ly$α$ RT equations for a static, uniform gas cloud under cylindrical geometry. The solution is verified through Ly$α$ Monte Carlo RT simulations, and compared to those under slab and spherical geometries in literature. Second, to characterise the recoil effect, we empirically modify recoil-free Ly$α$ spectra. The method is motivated by Ly$α$ RT equations with recoil and justified by simulations. Finally, we account for constant velocity gradients in Ly$α$ RT equations and obtain series solutions for Ly$α$ spectra. The solutions demonstrate good agreement to Ly$α$ spectra from simulations for small velocity gradients (i.e. edge velocity $v_{\rm E}$ of a cloud being comparable to the thermal velocity $b$) but become less accurate for large ones. To characterise Ly$α$ spectra under large velocity gradients, we empirically extend the functional form of solutions and constrain them from fitting simulated Ly$α$ spectra. The resulting fitting formulae show significant improvement for large velocity gradients ($v_{\rm E}/b \sim 100$) under large optical depths. The analytical study of Ly$α$ spectra in this work completes the set of solutions under simple geometries, provides physical insights for Ly$α$ RT under recoil and velocity gradient, and develops analytical tools for theoretical studies that require inputs from Ly$α$ RT.

AI.tldr: This paper provides analytical solutions to Lyman-alpha radiative transfer equations under cylindrical, slab, and spherical geometries, incorporating the effects of atomic recoil and gas bulk motion. The solutions are validated against Monte Carlo simulations, with empirical extensions for large velocity gradients.
AI.motivation: To develop complete analytical solutions for Lyα radiative transfer under simple geometries that include recoil and velocity gradient effects, providing physical insights and analytical tools for theoretical studies requiring Lyα RT inputs.
AI.method: Analytical solutions to Lyα RT equations for static uniform gas clouds under cylindrical geometry (verified via Monte Carlo simulations and compared to slab/spherical solutions); empirical modification of recoil-free spectra to account for recoil; series solutions incorporating constant velocity gradients, extended empirically for large gradients with fitting formulae constrained by simulations.
AI.result: Cylindrical geometry solutions verified against Monte Carlo simulations; recoil modification method justified by simulations; series solutions show good agreement for small velocity gradients (v_E/b ~ 1) but degrade for large ones; empirical fitting formulae significantly improve accuracy for large velocity gradients (v_E/b ~ 100) under large optical depths.
AI.conclusion: The analytical study completes the set of Lyα RT solutions under simple geometries, offers physical insights into recoil and velocity gradient effects, and provides useful analytical tools for broader theoretical applications.

title: Too shy to spin? Cosmic wallflowers as proto-globular clusters
comment: 9 pages, submitted to MNRAS
summary: We investigate the rotational properties of star-forming clusters at $z \sim 7.6$ in the high-resolution simulation MassiveBlackPS, focusing on two formation channels: clusters forming in galactic discs via gravitational instability and isolated circumgalactic systems, referred to as cosmic wallflowers, born out of cosmic filaments. Using stellar kinematics, we compare their rotational velocities, $v_{\rm rot}$, and rotational support, $v/σ$, to study whether formation environment leaves a clear dynamical imprint. We find a clear separation, wherein cosmic wallflowers systematically have lower rotational velocities and span a wide range in $v/σ$, whereas the identified disc clusters are strongly rotation-dominated and extend to higher $v_{\rm rot}$. When combined with stellar surface densities, a subset of the low-$v_{\rm rot}$ cosmic wallflowers lie surprisingly close to the observed globular cluster population in the Milky Way, whereas disc clusters remain offset. Within the cosmic wallflower population, we identify two regimes: lower-density, weakly rotating systems that overlap with these globular cluster properties, and denser, more rotationally supported systems that likely follow a different evolutionary pathway, possibly linking them to the origin of massive black hole seeds at high redshift. We further find that the gas content correlates with this behaviour, with gas-rich cosmic wallflowers preferentially occupying this low-rotation regime. This all suggests that environment and baryonic content together play a key role in setting the initial dynamical state and possible fate of clusters. In particular, weakly rotating, gas-rich cosmic wallflowers emerge as natural proto-globular cluster candidates, potentially evolving towards present-day systems through angular momentum loss and dynamical heating.

AI.tldr: Using high-resolution simulations, this study shows that star clusters at z~7.6 forming in galactic discs are rotation-dominated, while those formed in cosmic filaments ("cosmic wallflowers") have lower rotation and a subset overlap with observed Milky Way globular cluster properties, suggesting environment determines their dynamical evolution.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the formation environment (galactic disc vs. cosmic filaments) of high-redshift star clusters leaves a clear dynamical imprint on their rotational properties, and to identify potential proto-globular cluster candidates at z~7.6.
AI.method: High-resolution cosmological simulation MassiveBlackPS; analysis of stellar kinematics (v_rot, v/σ) of clusters at z~7.6; comparison of disc-formed clusters vs. circumgalactic "cosmic wallflowers" formed from cosmic filaments.
AI.result: Cosmic wallflowers have systematically lower rotational velocities and a wide range of v/σ; disc clusters are rotation-dominated with higher v_rot. Low-v_rot, gas-rich cosmic wallflowers overlap with Milky Way globular cluster properties, while disc clusters remain offset. Two regimes within wallflowers identified: low-density weakly rotating (proto-GC candidates) and denser, more rotationally supported systems (possible massive black hole seed hosts).
AI.conclusion: Environment and baryonic content jointly determine the initial dynamical state of high-z clusters. Weakly rotating, gas-rich cosmic wallflowers are natural proto-globular cluster candidates that may evolve into present-day globular clusters through angular momentum loss and dynamical heating.

title: SEEDZ: Rapid Galaxy Assembly as a Pathway to Supermassive Stars, Dense Stellar Environments and Massive Black Hole Seeds
comment: Submitted to the Open Journal of Astrophysics
summary: We investigate the assembly history of early galaxies in the SEEDZ hydrodynamic simulations, to investigate the high inflow rates believed to be required for the formation of supermassive stars (SMSs), dense stellar clusters and subsequently heavy seed black holes. Using a heavy seed formation criteria of $>$1 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ flowing into 10 pc regions, we find that heavy seeds form in halos that grow rapidly compared to those halos that never meet the criteria. Halos with growth rates of $\gtrsim$1 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ at their virial radius (scales of a few hundred pc) are able to sustain a flow rate of 0.1 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ into the inner 1 pc of the halo, maintaining higher density environments within the central 10 - 100~pc. These halos continue to grow rapidly after their initial collapse, typically forming heavy seeds $\sim$100 Myr after forming their first stars and stellar mass black holes. By $z=10$, most heavy seeds form in regions of near-solar metallicity, although a minority of heavy seeds do continue to form in low metallicity (10$^{-2}$ Z$_\odot$) regions. Under the assumption that a SMS forms as the progenitor to a heavy seed if it forms in a region of low (10$^{-2}$ Z$_\odot$) metallicity, and can sustain high accretion rates above 0.02 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ throughout the SMS lifetime of 2 Myr, we find a number density of SMSs of 0.1 cMpc$^{-3}$, meaning that only a fraction of 10$^{-4}$ of these SMSs would need to be visible to JWST to account for the observed population of Little Red Dot galaxies.

AI.tldr: Using SEEDZ simulations, the authors find that heavy seed black holes form in rapidly growing halos with high inflow rates, typically ~100 Myr after first star formation, and that only a tiny fraction (10⁻⁴) of supermassive stars need be visible to JWST to explain observed Little Red Dot galaxies.
AI.motivation: To investigate the assembly history of early galaxies and the high inflow rates believed necessary for forming supermassive stars, dense stellar clusters, and subsequently heavy seed black holes.
AI.method: Analysis of SEEDZ hydrodynamic simulations with a heavy seed formation criterion of >1 M☉ yr⁻¹ flowing into 10 pc regions, examining halo growth rates and inflow at virial radii and inner pc scales.
AI.result: Heavy seeds form in rapidly growing halos (≳1 M☉ yr⁻¹ at virial radius) that sustain 0.1 M☉ yr⁻¹ into inner 1 pc; most form at near-solar metallicity by z=10, with a minority in low metallicity (10⁻² Z☉) regions; SMS number density ~0.1 cMpc⁻³.
AI.conclusion: Only a fraction of 10⁻⁴ of these supermassive stars would need to be visible to JWST to account for the observed population of Little Red Dot galaxies.

title: JWST Reveals Compact Nuclear Starbursts Masquerading as AGNs in Metal-Poor Dwarfs: Where Are the Accreting Intermediate-Mass Black Holes?
comment: Comments welcome
summary: We present JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of the low-mass, metal-poor galaxy SDSS~J160135.95+311353.7 (J1601), selected for its extreme mid-infrared colors and compact nuclear emission, placing it within widely used WISE color diagnostics for active galactic nuclei (AGNs). Despite this selection, we find no evidence for coronal lines, X-ray emission, or variability typically associated with accretion activity. We compare J1601 to SDSS~J120122.30+021108.3 (J1201), a similar but lower-mass, more metal-poor system studied previously (Doan, 2025). Both galaxies host compact nuclear starbursts but differ in their stellar populations and dust properties: J1601 shows CO bandhead absorption indicative of red supergiants, weak nuclear Wolf--Rayet features, and a circumnuclear PAH ring, consistent with a more developed recent starburst, while J1201 is more dust-enshrouded and chemically primitive. Despite these differences, neither system shows evidence for AGN activity, indicating that the absence of accretion is not simply due to evolutionary timing. Photoionization models show that the weakness of high-ionization emission cannot be explained by low metallicity alone, implying a genuine deficit of hard ionizing photons. Crucially, the red mid-infrared colors in both systems originate from compact, unresolved nuclear emission confined to the nuclear star cluster. These results demonstrate that compact nuclear starbursts can mimic AGN-like mid-infrared colors without accretion, and that commonly used AGN diagnostics may not uniquely identify accreting black holes in metal-poor dwarf galaxies. Our findings suggest that such systems may not provide the conditions required for efficient black hole growth and/or may lie near or below the regime where black hole seeds can form.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of two low-mass, metal-poor galaxies (J1601 and J1201) with AGN-like mid-infrared colors reveals that their red mid-IR colors actually originate from compact nuclear starbursts rather than active galactic nuclei. Neither system shows evidence of AGN activity (no coronal lines, X-ray emission, or variability), and photoionization models indicate a genuine deficit of hard ionizing photons that cannot be explained by low metallicity alone. This demonstrates that compact nuclear starbursts can mimic AGN-like mid-IR colors, questioning commonly used AGN diagnostics in metal-poor dwarf galaxies and suggesting these systems may lack conditions for efficient black hole growth or black hole seed formation.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether low-mass, metal-poor dwarf galaxies with extreme mid-infrared colors (typically used as AGN diagnostics) actually host active galactic nuclei, or whether their emission can be explained by other phenomena such as compact nuclear starbursts.
AI.method: JWST/NIRSpec spectroscopy of J1601, comparison with previously studied J1201, photoionization modeling, and multi-wavelength analysis (X-ray, variability, coronal lines) to assess AGN presence.
AI.result: Neither galaxy shows evidence for AGN activity (no coronal lines, X-ray emission, or variability). The red mid-infrared colors originate from compact, unresolved nuclear emission confined to the nuclear star cluster. Photoionization models show the weakness of high-ionization emission reflects a genuine deficit of hard ionizing photons beyond what low metallicity can explain.
AI.conclusion: Compact nuclear starbursts can mimic AGN-like mid-infrared colors without accretion in metal-poor dwarf galaxies, challenging commonly used WISE-based AGN diagnostics. These systems may lack conditions for efficient black hole growth or may be near/below the regime where black hole seeds can form.

title: Discriminating blazar emission models with high-energy polarimetry: Multi-band predictions and detectability
summary: Polarimetric properties of blazars provide key constraints on the acceleration mechanisms powering their relativistic jets, the high-energy emission processes involved, and the composition of the jet itself. We present a multi-band polarimetric study spanning from soft X-rays to gamma-ray energies, considering several bands for current and future missions (0.275 keV, 2-8 keV, 0.5-10 keV, 6-35 keV, 0.2-5 MeV, and 1-100 GeV). Our sample is drawn from the RoboPol monitoring programme, a statistically complete gamma-ray sample including low-, intermediate-, and high-synchrotron-peaked blazars. Using spectral energy distribution fitting performed with the Bjet_MCMC tool, we give predictions on the flux expected for each source in the selected energy bands. We model the polarimetric signatures under three competing emission scenarios: leptonic, hadronic, and hybrid. The detectability of each source was assessed by accounting for the instruments' minimum detectable polarisation (MDP) and by computing the probability of the detection in a blind survey. We show that simultaneous multi-wavelength observations can effectively discriminate between competing emission models due to the difference in the expected polarisation degree. Finally, we derive sensitivity requirements for future gamma-ray polarimetric missions aimed at increasing the number of detectable sources.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a multi-band polarimetric study of blazars from soft X-rays to gamma rays, using the RoboPol sample and Bjet_MCMC spectral fitting to predict fluxes. It compares leptonic, hadronic, and hybrid emission models, assesses detectability via MDP, and demonstrates that simultaneous multi-wavelength polarimetry can distinguish between competing emission scenarios, providing sensitivity requirements for future gamma-ray polarimetric missions.
AI.motivation: To constrain acceleration mechanisms, high-energy emission processes, and jet composition in blazars using polarimetric properties across a broad energy range (soft X-rays to gamma rays), and to determine which emission scenario (leptonic, hadronic, or hybrid) is most consistent with observations.
AI.method: The authors use the statistically complete RoboPol gamma-ray sample (including LSP, ISP, HSP blazars), perform spectral energy distribution fitting with Bjet_MCMC to predict fluxes in six bands (0.275 keV to 100 GeV), model polarimetric signatures under three competing scenarios (leptonic, hadronic, hybrid), and assess detectability using minimum detectable polarisation (MDP) and blind survey detection probabilities.
AI.result: Simultaneous multi-wavelength polarimetric observations can effectively discriminate between leptonic, hadronic, and hybrid emission models due to differences in predicted polarisation degree. Detectability varies by source and instrument sensitivity, and sensitivity requirements for future gamma-ray polarimetric missions are derived.
AI.conclusion: Multi-band polarimetry is a powerful diagnostic tool for blazar jet physics. Future gamma-ray polarimetric missions should be designed with sensitivity sufficient to increase the number of detectable sources, enabling model discrimination.

title: The Bright Future of the Dark and Dim Universe
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKAII (AASKAII),2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Bourke01
summary: This chapter investigates the low-mass frontier of galaxy formation through two complementary populations: the starless Reionization-Limited HI Clouds (RELHICs) that trace the ``dark'' Universe, and the faint, gas-rich galaxies that define the ``dim'' Universe. RELHICs offer pristine laboratories for probing the distribution of DM on sub-galactic scales, providing a direct test of the Lambda Cold Dark Matter ($Λ$CDM) model predictions. The dim Universe provides statistical constraints on cosmology, galaxy formation and evolution, as well as baryoninc physics through key observables including the low-mass end of the neutral-hydrogen mass function (HIMF), the neutral-hydrogen velocity function (HIVF), and the low-mass end of the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation (bTFR). This chapter outlines core science questions that can be tackled leveraging radio observations of both the dark and dim Universe. Additionally, it outlines strategies to identify RELHICs amid tidal or pressure-confined contaminants, while providing observational predictions for the dim Universe. The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) in its mid-frequency Array Assembly 4 (AA4) configuration will, for the first time, resolve the internal gas structure of nearby RELHICs and build deep, wide-area datasets that definitively constrain the HIMF, HIVF, and bTFR down to masses of $10^{6}~\msol$ -- offering a complete observational framework to test the $Λ$CDM paradigm and the baryonic processes that shape the faint end of galaxy formation.

AI.tldr: This chapter explores the low-mass frontier of galaxy formation by studying starless RELHICs (probing dark matter on sub-galactic scales) and faint gas-rich galaxies (constraining cosmology and baryonic physics). It outlines science strategies for identifying RELHICs and provides observational predictions, highlighting that SKA's AA4 configuration will resolve gas structure in RELHICs and build deep datasets to constrain key relations (HIMF, HIVF, bTFR) down to 10^6 M⊙, testing ΛCDM and baryonic processes at the faint end.
AI.motivation: To investigate the low-mass frontier of galaxy formation by using two complementary populations—starless RELHICs (probing the "dark" Universe) and faint gas-rich galaxies (probing the "dim" Universe)—to test ΛCDM predictions and constrain baryonic physics at sub-galactic scales.
AI.method: Leveraging radio observations (specifically SKA AA4) to identify and characterize RELHICs, distinguish them from tidal/pressure-confined contaminants, and build deep, wide-area datasets to measure the HIMF, HIVF, and bTFR down to 10^6 M⊙.
AI.result: SKA AA4 will resolve the internal gas structure of nearby RELHICs and provide definitive constraints on the HIMF, HIVF, and bTFR at masses as low as 10^6 M⊙, offering a complete observational framework for testing ΛCDM.
AI.conclusion: The combination of RELHICs and dim galaxies provides a powerful observational test of the ΛCDM paradigm and baryonic processes that govern the faint end of galaxy formation.

title: Impact of neutrino-electron scattering and an improved treatment of pair processes on binary neutron star mergers
comment: 25p, 22 figures, version released for comments before journal submission
summary: Multimessenger observations of neutron star mergers are unique opportunities to constrain the properties of dense matter and the production site of heavy nuclei. To leverage these observations, we require reliable models of the electromagnetic signals powered by mergers. An important limitation to our ability to develop such models is the use of approximate neutrino physics in simulations. Here, we present simulations using an improved version of our Monte Carlo transport algorithm specifically designed to allow for more advanced on-the-fly calculations of reaction rates that use the simulated energy distribution of neutrinos, including in blocking factors, while still relying on approximations for the angular distribution of neutrinos. We use these new methods to include in simulations inelastic scattering of neutrinos on electrons, and to improve our treatment of neutrino-antineutrino pair annihilation. We find that, without increasing the cost of simulations, we can marginally get to the point when the addition of a single packet represents a change $Δf_ν<1$ in the angle-integrated distribution function, at the cost of increased shot noise in the coupling to the fluid. With inelastic scattering and a better treatment of pair processes, we find a reduction in the average energy and total luminosity of heavy-lepton neutrinos, and an increase in the amount of mass ejected -- here by $50\%$, although on a relatively low amount of total ejected mass $<0.005M_\odot$. In a separate set of simulations varying the total mass of the binary away from its prompt collapse threshold, we find rapid variations in the amount of ejected matter and in the geometry and composition of the outflows with the total mass of the system. Finally, we use the simulations with our more advanced transport scheme to study in more detail the energy spectrum of neutrinos across the merger remnant.

AI.tldr: This paper presents improved Monte Carlo neutrino transport simulations for neutron star mergers, incorporating inelastic scattering on electrons and better pair annihilation treatment, finding a 50% increase in ejected mass and revealing rapid variations in outflow properties with system mass.
AI.motivation: To constrain dense matter properties and heavy nuclei production sites via multimessenger observations of neutron star mergers, reliable electromagnetic signal models are needed, but current simulations are limited by approximate neutrino physics.
AI.method: Improved Monte Carlo transport algorithm with on-the-fly reaction rate calculations using simulated neutrino energy distributions, including blocking factors and angular distribution approximations; incorporates inelastic neutrino-electron scattering and improved neutrino-antineutrino pair annihilation treatment.
AI.result: Without increased simulation cost, angle-integrated distribution function changes Δf_ν < 1 per packet addition but with increased shot noise. Inelastic scattering and better pair processes reduce heavy-lepton neutrino average energy and luminosity, and increase ejected mass by 50% (though <0.005M_⊙ total). Rapid variations in ejected matter, outflow geometry, and composition found near prompt collapse threshold.
AI.conclusion: Advanced neutrino transport improves accuracy of merger simulations and reveals sensitive dependence of outflows on system mass, motivating further study of neutrino energy spectra across merger remnants.

title: Self-interacting dark matter promotes bar formation in disk galaxies
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, submitted to MNRAS. Comments welcome!
summary: Despite its remarkable success on large scales, the standard $Λ$CDM paradigm faces persistent small-scale challenges that have motivated alternative models for the dark sector. Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) offers a compelling possibility, in which dark matter particles can scatter off each other. Stellar bars are a ubiquitous feature of disk galaxies across cosmic time. Bars are dynamically coupled to their host galaxy's dark matter halo, and therefore their properties provide a powerful probe of the nature and distribution of dark matter. In this paper, we use idealized, high-resolution $N$-body simulations and analytic calculations based on kinetic theory to study bar formation and evolution in disk galaxies embedded in SIDM halos. We find that compared with collisionless CDM, SIDM produces bars that form earlier and grow to larger amplitudes, even for modest self-interaction cross sections. In several cases, disks that remain stable in CDM, including kinematically hot and dark-matter-dominated disks, develop strong bars in SIDM. This accelerated bar growth occurs because self-interactions broaden the bar-halo resonances and enhance angular momentum transfer from the stellar disk to the halo. We explicitly show that this phenomenon is not related to core formation in SIDM halos. At late times, gravothermal core collapse can raise the central dark matter density enough to weaken or dissolve the bar. These results suggest that the abundance, strength, and redshift evolution of barred galaxies offer a promising observational route to constraining dark matter self-interactions, particularly in light of the growing sample of high-redshift bars revealed by JWST.

AI.tldr: Using N-body simulations and analytic calculations, this paper finds that self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) causes stellar bars to form earlier and grow stronger compared to collisionless CDM, even in disks that would remain stable in CDM. Self-interactions broaden bar-halo resonances and enhance angular momentum transfer. Late-time gravothermal collapse can weaken bars. This offers an observational route to constraining dark matter self-interactions via barred galaxies.
AI.motivation: The small-scale challenges of ΛCDM motivate alternative dark sector models like SIDM. Stellar bars are dynamically coupled to dark matter halos and thus serve as sensitive probes of dark matter properties, motivating the study of bar evolution in SIDM.
AI.method: Idealized, high-resolution N-body simulations combined with analytic calculations based on kinetic theory to study bar formation and evolution in disk galaxies embedded in SIDM halos.
AI.result: SIDM produces bars that form earlier and grow to larger amplitudes than in CDM, even for modest cross sections. Disks stable in CDM (kinematically hot or dark-matter-dominated) develop strong bars in SIDM. This is not due to core formation. Late-time gravothermal collapse can raise central density enough to weaken/dissolve bars.
AI.conclusion: The abundance, strength, and redshift evolution of barred galaxies offer a promising observational route to constraining dark matter self-interactions, especially given high-redshift bar samples from JWST.

title: A hidden ultra-relativistic spine in the jet of a neutrino-associated blazar
comment: submitted; comments are welcome
summary: Supermassive black holes launch powerful jets of plasma that can accelerate particles to extreme energies, but the physical conditions required to produce high-energy neutrinos remain unknown. In the blazar TXS 0506+056, the first source individually linked to a high-energy neutrino, radio images had seemed to reveal a jet too slow to sustain the extreme conditions required for neutrino production. Here we resolve this tension using long-term radio monitoring, particularly Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) imaging. We uncover a disturbance in emission propagating with an apparent speed of 21+-1 times the speed of light, that is masked by slower, radio-bright features that dominated earlier analyses. We interpret this as the signature of a stratified jet: an ultra-relativistic spine with Lorentz factor Gamma>20 embedded within a slower outer sheath. As the disturbance travels along the spine, it progressively illuminates the sheath, producing the delayed radio flare and naturally accounting for the years-long offset between neutrino and radio emission. The same pattern recurs in a second neutrino-associated event, pointing to a repeatable multi-messenger engine. These findings challenge the standard interpretation of VLBI jet speeds and establish a concrete, testable framework connecting structured jets to the sources of the Universe's highest-energy neutrinos.

AI.tldr: Radio observations reveal that the blazar TXS 0506+056 hosts a stratified jet with an ultra-relativistic spine (Lorentz factor Γ>20) masked by a slower sheath, resolving the apparent speed discrepancy. A disturbance propagating at 21±1c along the spine produces delayed radio flares that align with years-long offsets between neutrino and radio emission, establishing a repeatable multi-messenger connection.
AI.motivation: To resolve the tension between high-energy neutrino production from blazar TXS 0506+056 and earlier radio imaging that suggested jet speeds too slow to sustain the extreme conditions required for neutrino production.
AI.method: Long-term radio monitoring using Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) imaging to track emission disturbances and measure apparent superluminal speeds.
AI.result: Discovered a disturbance propagating at 21±1c, masked by slower radio-bright features. This reveals a stratified jet with an ultra-relativistic spine (Γ>20) inside a slower outer sheath, where the disturbance illuminates the sheath progressively, causing delayed radio flares.
AI.conclusion: The findings challenge standard VLBI jet speed interpretations and establish a testable framework linking structured jets to high-energy neutrino sources, with a repeatable pattern observed in a second neutrino-associated event.

title: The Impact and Environment of Massive Stars and Stellar Clusters
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv: 2606.20366)
summary: Massive stars and stellar clusters shape galactic evolution through powerful feedback mechanisms including radiation pressure, photoionization, stellar winds, and cosmic ray acceleration. However, their impact remains poorly understood due to observational challenges: they are rare, distant on average, and deeply embedded within dense, dusty environments. Radio observations provide a unique window into these processes, as radio emission penetrates obscuring material and traces both thermal free-free emission from ionized gas and non-thermal synchrotron emission from shocks and particle acceleration. The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will revolutionize massive star studies through unprecedented sensitivity and angular resolution. SKA observations will enable detailed characterization of hierarchical structures within HII regions, measurements of physical conditions through hydrogen, helium, and carbon radio recombination lines (RRLs), and detection of non-thermal emission from cosmic ray acceleration in star-forming regions. SKA will permit systematic measurements of stellar wind mass-loss rates, studies of photoionized gas kinematics and dynamics, and exploration of photodissociation regions surrounding ultracompact HII regions. Additionally, magnetic field strengths can be probed through Zeeman effect observations of RRLs. This chapter discusses the current understanding of massive stars and stellar clusters and their feedback processes. We highlight how SKA observations will advance our knowledge of massive star formation, stellar winds, hierarchical structures in HII regions, cosmic ray acceleration, and magnetic field regulation of star formation - providing crucial insights into feedback mechanisms governing the structure and evolution of the Milky Way and galaxies.

AI.tldr: Massive stars and stellar clusters drive galactic feedback (radiation, winds, cosmic rays), but are hard to observe. Radio observations (free-free, synchrotron) pierce dusty environments. The SKA will revolutionize the field by enabling detailed measurements of HII region structures, RRLs, stellar winds, non-thermal emission, and magnetic fields via Zeeman effect, advancing understanding of star formation and galactic evolution.
AI.motivation: Massive stars and stellar clusters play a crucial role in galactic evolution through feedback mechanisms (radiation pressure, photoionization, stellar winds, cosmic ray acceleration), but their impact is poorly understood due to observational challenges—they are rare, distant, and deeply embedded in dense dusty environments.
AI.method: The Square Kilometre Array (SKA) will provide unprecedented sensitivity and angular resolution for radio observations, enabling characterization of hierarchical HII region structures, physical condition measurements via H/He/C radio recombination lines, detection of non-thermal synchrotron emission from cosmic ray acceleration, measurements of stellar wind mass-loss rates, kinematic and dynamical studies of photoionized gas, exploration of photodissociation regions around ultracompact HII regions, and magnetic field probing via Zeeman effect on RRLs.
AI.result: SKA observations will advance knowledge of massive star formation, stellar winds, hierarchical structures in HII regions, cosmic ray acceleration, and magnetic field regulation of star formation.
AI.conclusion: SKA will provide crucial insights into feedback mechanisms governing the structure and evolution of the Milky Way and galaxies.

title: Gamma-ray Bursts in the Radio Sky: the Role of the SKA-VLBI
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no: AASKAII/Giarratana01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: Radio observations of $γ$-ray bursts (GRBs) employing the very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) technique provide us with fundamental information on the dynamics and the geometry of the GRB blast wave. With its high angular resolution ($\sim$milli-arcsecond), VLBI allows us to measure the apparent superluminal expansion, to characterise the structure of the jet and to constrain the viewing angle and jet opening angle. While this information is crucial to understand these transient events, such studies have been possible only for three GRBs to date, owing to both the poor sensitivity of current radio facilities and the paucity of close and bright GRBs. In this chapter, we estimate the impact that the SKA-Mid will have on these studies, when included in a VLBI network. We performed a series of dedicated simulations of VLBI observations of GRBs, considering five VLBI networks and the SKA-Mid, both in its AA* and AA4 configurations. We show that including the SKA-Mid in a global-VLBI experiment will: (i) allow us to measure the size and the expansion of a GRB up to a redshift $z\simeq 0.25$ (at a confidence level of $3σ$); (ii) constrain the size $\gtrsim$2 times better than the current global-VLBI array; (iii) improve the localisation precision in Declination from 4 to 30 times; (iv) detect the apparent proper motion of GRBs seen slightly off-axis with a confidence level 3 times better than current VLBI networks. Ultimately, the SKA-Mid will open a new window on a portion of the GRB population that has been inaccessible so far.

AI.tldr: This paper estimates the impact of the SKA-Mid (AA* and AA4 configurations) on VLBI observations of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), showing it will improve size measurement (up to z~0.25 at 3σ), constrain jet size ~2x better, improve declination localization 4-30x, and detect off-axis proper motion 3x better than current VLBI networks, opening access to a previously inaccessible GRB population.
AI.motivation: Current VLBI studies of GRBs are limited to only three events due to poor sensitivity of radio facilities and scarcity of bright, close GRBs. This motivates the need to assess whether future instruments like SKA-Mid can overcome these limitations and enable systematic studies of GRB blast wave dynamics and geometry.
AI.method: The authors performed dedicated simulations of VLBI observations of GRBs, considering five VLBI networks and the SKA-Mid in both its AA* and AA4 configurations, evaluating performance metrics such as size measurement, localization precision, and proper motion detection.
AI.result: Including SKA-Mid in a global-VLBI experiment will: (i) measure GRB size/expansion up to z~0.25 at 3σ; (ii) constrain size ~2x better than current arrays; (iii) improve Declination localization by 4-30x; (iv) detect apparent proper motion of slightly off-axis GRBs 3x better than current networks.
AI.conclusion: The SKA-Mid will open a new observational window on a previously inaccessible portion of the GRB population, enabling VLBI studies of GRB dynamics and structure at significantly greater distances and precision than currently possible.

title: Discovery of an extremely narrow trail-like feature crossing the Veil Supernova Remnant in deep amateur observations
comment: 8 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables
summary: We report the discovery of an extremely narrow and highly collimated gaseous trail-like structure crossing the eastern region of the Veil Nebula (Cygnus Loop). The feature was first identified in deep narrow-band H-alpha images obtained by a small telescope and was confirmed in more than a dozen publicly available amateur and professional images in the last two decades, rejecting the possibility of being an artifact (e.g., artificial satellite trail). To characterize its structural and luminosity parameters, we applied a model-fitting code originally developed for the analysis of extragalactic stellar tidal streams. The structure is only detected in H-alpha emission, with no detectable counterpart in [SII] or in visible observations, and shows an almost constant brightness and width along its extension. It exhibits a surface brightness of 22.32+/- 0.13 H-alpha mag arcsec^2. Model fitting yields a median width of 1.63", which corresponds to a physical scale of approximately 1200 UA, assuming it is at the same distance (2400 light-years) as the Veil Nebula remnant. We discuss several potential scenarios for the origin of this feature: a Herbig-Haro-like jet, the trail of a high-velocity object, or a non-radiative shock associated with the supernova remnant. We rule out the Herbig-Haro scenario, given the absence of a driving stellar source and the lack of [S II] emission. A high-velocity-object wake cannot yet be excluded, particularly if the driver is a compact remnant, but the absence of an obvious source or bow-shock apex and the extremely small, nearly constant width of the structure make a normal runaway-star origin unlikely. The current evidence instead favours a Balmer-dominated non-radiative shock associated with the Cygnus Loop, generated as the SNR blast wave encounters a dense material layer or magnetic structure viewed nearly edge-on.

AI.tldr: Discovery of a narrow, collimated H-alpha trail in the Veil Nebula (Cygnus Loop). The structure is ~1.63" wide, detected only in H-alpha, with no [SII] counterpart. Analysis rules out a Herbig-Haro jet and a normal runaway star; the most plausible explanation is a Balmer-dominated non-radiative shock from the SNR blast wave interacting with a dense or magnetized layer viewed edge-on.
AI.motivation: To characterize a newly discovered extremely narrow gaseous trail in the Veil Nebula and determine its physical origin, given its unusual morphology and emission characteristics.
AI.method: Discovery via deep narrow-band H-alpha imaging; confirmation across multiple amateur/professional datasets to rule out artifacts; application of a tidal-stream model-fitting code to quantify structural and luminosity parameters; multi-wavelength comparison (H-alpha, [SII], optical).
AI.result: Structure detected only in H-alpha, surface brightness 22.32±0.13 mag arcsec², median width 1.63" (~1200 AU at 2400 ly distance), nearly constant brightness and width along its length.
AI.conclusion: Herbig-Haro jet and normal runaway-star trails are ruled out; a Balmer-dominated non-radiative shock associated with the Cygnus Loop SNR, viewed nearly edge-on, is the favored interpretation.

title: Parsec-scale polarimetry and kinematics of a spine-sheath jet in the neutrino-blazar TXS 0506+056
comment: 13 pages, 8 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: In 2017, the blazar TXS 0506+056 showed a remarkable gamma-ray outburst simultaneously with a high-energy neutrino detection by IceCube from the same sky region. The significance of this association was found to be on the order of 3 sigma thus providing a strong link between the neutrino emission and the blazar flare. The high-energy flare in TXS 0506+056 was followed by a delayed radio flare, peaking in $\sim2020$ in the aftermath of the neutrino event. We investigate the parsec-scale jet structure and dynamics of TXS 0506+056 using 15 GHz full-polarization VLBI observations obtained between 2009 and 2025 with the Very Long Baseline Array. Our kinematic analysis reveals moderate superluminal jet speeds of $\sim(1-2)$c and two quasi-stationary components. A new jet component with comparable speed was ejected contemporaneously with the 2017 IceCube neutrino event. The stacked polarization map is consistent with a stratified spine-sheath jet structure: an inner spine with EVPA aligned with the jet, surrounded by a sheath layer with perpendicular EVPA. Variability in total intensity and polarization further indicates interaction between these layers, particularly evident in characteristic linear polarization flares, associated with EVPA rotations of the quasi-stationary components. The multi-layered jet configuration is consistent with previous studies that were able to explain the neutrino emission in this TXS 0506+056 through a spine-sheath jet structure. We suggest that TXS 0506+056 represents an archetypal case and that similar polarization signatures and geometric light curve flares may be present in other neutrino-emitting sources, potentially offering a solution to the Doppler-crisis phenomenon observed in TeV-emitting blazars.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes 16 years of VLBI observations (2009–2025) of blazar TXS 0506+056, linking its 2017 neutrino event to a new jet component ejection and revealing a stratified spine-sheath jet structure through full-polarization imaging.
AI.motivation: To investigate the parsec-scale jet structure and dynamics of TXS 0506+056, the first blazar associated with a high-energy neutrino (IceCube-170922A), and understand the physical mechanisms linking neutrino production to jet activity.
AI.method: 15 GHz full-polarization VLBI observations with the Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA) over 2009–2025, including kinematic analysis, polarization stacking, and total intensity/polarization variability studies.
AI.result: Moderate superluminal speeds (~1–2c) and two quasi-stationary components; a new component ejected contemporaneously with the 2017 neutrino event; stacked polarization map reveals a stratified spine-sheath structure (inner spine with EVPA aligned with jet, sheath with perpendicular EVPA); linear polarization flares with EVPA rotations in quasi-stationary components indicate layer interactions.
AI.conclusion: TXS 0506+056 is an archetypal neutrino-emitting blazar with a spine-sheath jet structure; similar polarization and geometric light curve signatures may be present in other neutrino sources, potentially resolving the Doppler-crisis in TeV blazars.

title: A Definitive Determination of the Interstellar Carbon Abundance toward rho Ophiuchi A and B
comment: 8 pages, 3 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ Letters
summary: We present the results of an effort to derive interstellar gas-phase C II abundances along the lines of sight toward rho Oph A and B. Our analysis is based on high-resolution NUV and FUV archival spectra acquired with the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph on the Hubble Space Telescope. Column densities of C II are derived both from fits to the weak C II] 2325 intersystem transition and from fits to the damping wings of the strong C II 1334 line. We find that the results from the weak-line and strong-line determinations agree with each other remarkably well for both sight lines, demonstrating the reliability of the f-values of the C II transitions. Furthermore, the gas-phase C abundance that we obtain for rho Oph A is in very good agreement with previous determinations of interstellar C abundances from measurements of the weak C II] 2325 line. By demonstrating the reliability of the damping wing fitting technique for the C II 1334 line, our analysis opens the door to future surveys of interstellar C abundances using the same methodology.

AI.tldr: The paper derives interstellar gas-phase C II abundances toward rho Oph A and B using HST/STIS archival spectra, showing excellent agreement between weak-line (C II] 2325) and strong-line (C II 1334 damping wings) methods, validating both the atomic data and the damping wing fitting technique for future interstellar carbon abundance surveys.
AI.motivation: To derive reliable interstellar gas-phase C II abundances and validate the damping wing fitting technique for the C II 1334 line as a robust method for future abundance surveys.
AI.method: High-resolution NUV and FUV archival spectra from HST/STIS; column densities derived from fitting the weak C II] 2325 intersystem transition and the damping wings of the strong C II 1334 line.
AI.result: Results from weak-line and strong-line determinations agree remarkably well for both sight lines; gas-phase C abundance for rho Oph A matches previous determinations from the C II] 2325 line.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates the reliability of the damping wing fitting technique for C II 1334, enabling future large-scale interstellar carbon abundance surveys using this methodology.

title: Modelling Dissipative Dynamics of r-mode Instability in Hybrid Stars
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures
summary: Compact star cores reach extreme densities and may contain exotic dense-matter phases. Information about the exotic interiors of rapidly rotating pulsars can be inferred from r-mode oscillations, whose stability is governed by viscous dissipation. In this work, we model a compact star containing a possible mixed phase of hadronic and quark matter and employ a hybrid statistical framework based on Bayesian inference to infer the dissipation time scales associated with the hybrid phase. Using low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXB) timing observations together with mass-radius constraints from the Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER) mission, we estimate the shear and bulk viscosity contributions to r-mode damping for a hybrid star of two layers. Our inference yields shear and bulk viscous dissipation time scales of $τ_s=(4.99^{+0.49}_{-0.52}) \times 10^8 T^{\frac{5}{3}}$s and $τ_B=(2.150^{+1.23}_{-0.60}) \times 10^{19} (T^4 10^{-12}+T^2 10^{-6})^{-1}Ω^{-2}$s respectively. The timescales thus obtained can be implemented to obtain the minima of the star's rotation frequency at $Ω=451.87$ Hz at temperature $T=0.259$ MeV for a hybrid star of mass $1.5$ $M_{\odot}$ and $Ω=517.47$ Hz at $T=0.234$ MeV for $M=1.75 M_{\odot}$. We find that the instability window obtained through the inference framework effectively explains the observed stability of millisecond pulsars in both the radio and LMXB populations, particularly for XTE J0929-314 and XTE J1807-294, J0437-4715, J2124-3358, respectively. These results demonstrate that Bayesian inference combined with r-mode phenomenology provides a powerful and observationally consistent framework for constraining the transport properties of dense hybrid matter.

AI.tldr: The paper uses Bayesian inference and r-mode oscillation data to constrain viscous dissipation timescales in hybrid stars (hadronic+quark matter), finding shear and bulk viscosity parameters that explain the stability of millisecond pulsars like XTE J0929-314 and XTE J1807-294.
AI.motivation: Compact star cores may contain exotic dense-matter phases, and r-mode oscillations—whose stability is governed by viscous dissipation—serve as a probe of these interiors. The authors aim to infer dissipation timescales in hybrid stars to understand pulsar stability.
AI.method: The authors model a two-layer hybrid star (hadronic+quark mixed phase) and employ a Bayesian inference framework using LMXB timing observations and NICER mass-radius constraints to estimate shear and bulk viscosity contributions to r-mode damping.
AI.result: Shear viscosity timescale: τ_s = (4.99^{+0.49}_{-0.52}) × 10^8 T^{5/3} s; bulk viscosity timescale: τ_B = (2.150^{+1.23}_{-0.60}) × 10^{19} (T^4 10^{-12}+T^2 10^{-6})^{-1} Ω^{-2} s. Minimum rotation frequencies: Ω=451.87 Hz at T=0.259 MeV (M=1.5 M⊙) and Ω=517.47 Hz at T=0.234 MeV (M=1.75 M⊙).
AI.conclusion: The inferred instability window explains the observed stability of millisecond pulsars, and Bayesian inference combined with r-mode phenomenology provides a powerful framework for constraining transport properties of dense hybrid matter.

title: OzSSy1: The Australian Southern Seyfert-1 Spectroscopic Atlas and Catalogue at z < 0.1
comment: Submitted to MNRAS, 21 pages, 16 figures, and 2 tables
summary: We present a spectroscopic atlas of 887 broad-line active galactic nuclei (AGNs) in the Southern sky, spanning redshifts $z < 0.1$, declinations $δ< 0$ deg and Galactic latitudes $|b| > 10$ deg. The sample aims at being a largely complete census of nearby broad-line AGN. The atlas is constructed from observations with $R\sim3000$ using the integral-field Wide Field Spectrograph at the Australian National University 2.3 m telescope. Spectra are extracted in a 6.7 arcsec aperture and have a median signal-to-noise ratio of 13 and 23 per Angstrom in the blue and red arms, respectively. Each spectrum is accompanied by a spectral decomposition that models the AGN continuum and host galaxy, along with fits to the emission lines H$γ$, H$β$, H$α$, He II, He I, [O III], [O I], [N II] and [S II], including broad Balmer and Helium components. The data products are publicly available and designed to support studies of population demographics and AGN variability in conjunction with future time-domain surveys.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a spectroscopic atlas of 887 broad-line AGNs in the Southern sky with R~3000 spectra from the Wide Field Spectrograph, including spectral decompositions and emission line fits, publicly available for population and variability studies.
AI.motivation: To create a largely complete census of nearby broad-line AGNs in the Southern sky, providing publicly available spectroscopic data and spectral decompositions to support population demographic studies and AGN variability research in conjunction with future time-domain surveys.
AI.method: Observations with R~3000 using the integral-field Wide Field Spectrograph at the ANU 2.3 m telescope; spectra extracted in 6.7 arcsec aperture; spectral decomposition modeling AGN continuum and host galaxy; emission line fitting for Hγ, Hβ, Hα, He II, He I, [O III], [O I], [N II], [S II] including broad Balmer and Helium components.
AI.result: A sample of 887 broad-line AGNs at z<0.1 in the Southern sky (δ<0°, |b|>10°) with median S/N of 13 (blue) and 23 (red) per Angstrom; all data products publicly available.
AI.conclusion: This atlas provides a comprehensive spectroscopic resource for nearby broad-line AGN studies, enabling population demographic analyses and serving as a baseline for AGN variability studies with upcoming time-domain surveys.

title: The Astrophysics of Fast Radio Bursts
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/Curtin01
summary: Fast radio bursts (FRBs) provide a glimpse of high-energy astrophysical phenomena in other galaxies. They point the way to extreme conditions that are currently undetectable by any other known means. These coherent radio flashes have timescales of microseconds to milliseconds, and inferred energies that are comparable to those of the most extreme bursts seen from Galactic neutron stars. However, the nature of FRB sources remains an open question in astrophysics. Magnetically powered neutron stars known as `magnetars' are a leading candidate for explaining the FRB phenomenon, but other plausible progenitors include magnetically interacting neutron-star binaries or accreting black holes. The diversity of FRB burst types and their galactic environments hint that multiple mechanisms and progenitor types may be responsible. Here we discuss the ways in which the SKA can uncover the nature of FRBs. In particular, we focus on the key advantages of the SKA: its Southern Hemisphere location and hence overlapping sky coverage with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, its high sensitivity compared to existing wide-field FRB surveys, its fast search timescales down to tens of $μ$s, and its broad spectral coverage with bands from 50 MHz to 15 GHz. With these capabilities, the SKA will excel in detecting FRB sources across new frequency ranges and timescales. This will aid in a better understanding of the fundamental astrophysics behind FRBs, which will in turn also contribute to their use as cosmological probes, as explored in companion chapters.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses how the Square Kilometre Array (SKA) can uncover the nature of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) through its Southern Hemisphere location, high sensitivity, fast search timescales, and broad spectral coverage, enabling detection across new frequency ranges and timescales to better understand FRB astrophysics and their use as cosmological probes.
AI.motivation: The nature of FRB sources remains an open question in astrophysics, with possible progenitors including magnetars, neutron-star binaries, or accreting black holes, motivating the need for advanced observational capabilities to identify the mechanisms behind these high-energy phenomena.
AI.method: The paper outlines the key advantages of the SKA for FRB research: its Southern Hemisphere location for overlapping sky coverage with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, high sensitivity exceeding existing wide-field FRB surveys, fast search timescales down to tens of microseconds, and broad spectral coverage from 50 MHz to 15 GHz.
AI.result: The SKA will excel in detecting FRB sources across new frequency ranges and timescales, providing capabilities that surpass existing surveys.
AI.conclusion: The SKA's capabilities will aid in better understanding the fundamental astrophysics behind FRBs, which will also contribute to their use as cosmological probes.

title: Mapping the Milky Way with Masers
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/XuYe01. Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary: SKA-VLBI is poised to revolutionize our understanding of the Galactic structure through its unprecedented astrometric precision and sensitivity. As a next-generation facility, it will answer long-standing questions about the Galactic structure by mapping its entire spiral structure in detail, spanning from the solar neighborhood, through the Galactic Center, to the far side of the Milky Way. Its access to the Southern sky will allow us to obtain more precise 3D parameters of the Galactic bar, reveal the nature of the 3-kpc Arm, and clarify the dynamical coupling between the bar and the spiral arms. By leveraging high-precision astrometry of numerous celestial objects with SKA-VLBI, the Galactic fundamental parameters such as the Solar motion and the Galactic rotation curve can be constrained more precisely. These advancements will not only elucidate the structure of our Milky Way, but also provide benchmarks for understanding barred spiral galaxies in general. Furthermore, they are important for advancing our knowledge of cosmological structure formation. The capabilities of SKA-VLBI will open a new era of high precision Galactic astrometry.

AI.tldr: This paper discusses how SKA-VLBI will revolutionize Galactic structure studies through unprecedented astrometric precision, mapping the Milky Way's spiral structure, bar, and fundamental parameters from the solar neighborhood to the far side.
AI.motivation: To answer long-standing questions about Galactic structure by leveraging SKA-VLBI's next-generation astrometric capabilities to map the Milky Way in unprecedented detail, especially in the Southern sky.
AI.method: Using SKA-VLBI's high-precision astrometry to measure 3D parameters of the Galactic bar, spiral arms, Solar motion, and rotation curve across the entire Milky Way, including the Galactic Center and far side.
AI.result: SKA-VLBI will obtain precise 3D parameters of the Galactic bar, reveal the nature of the 3-kpc Arm, clarify dynamical coupling between bar and spiral arms, and constrain Solar motion and Galactic rotation curve more precisely.
AI.conclusion: SKA-VLBI will open a new era of high-precision Galactic astrometry, providing benchmarks for understanding barred spiral galaxies and advancing knowledge of cosmological structure formation.

title: Exploring the physics behind the observed magnetic filaments in large scale radio galaxies
comment: Published in Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII), 2026 (arXiv:2606.20366). Advancing Astrophysics with the SKA II (AASKAII) outlines the transformative scientific advances that will be enabled by the SKA telescopes
summary:
Recent low-frequency MeerKAT observations of radio galaxies have revealed an unexpected population of thin, highly collimated synchrotron threads, whose numbers continue to grow with increasing survey depth and sensitivity. These intricate structures display a remarkable diversity of morphologies -- appearing as narrow filaments linking jets and lobes, as well as ring- or ribbon-like features embedded within the jets and radio lobes. Despite their ubiquity, the physical origin and stability of these collimated synchrotron threads remain poorly understood. Proposed mechanisms include shock compression and interactions with the magneto-ionic intracluster medium, magnetic flux tube formation, and reconnection-driven magnetic filaments.
  In this work, we investigate the formation and evolution of such magnetic filaments using three-dimensional, two-temperature general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations of realistically launched jets from supermassive black holes. From these simulations, we compute synthetic synchrotron emission maps and polarisation signatures, allowing us to predict the observable characteristics including morphology, brightness profiles, and polarisation patterns. Finally, we assess the detectability and diagnostic potential of these signatures with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory (SKAO), outlining how upcoming SKA observations can distinguish between competing physical models and illuminate the magnetic origin of the collimated synchrotron threads revealed by MeerKAT observations.

AI.tldr: Using 3D GRMHD simulations of jets from supermassive black holes, the authors model the formation of collimated synchrotron threads seen in MeerKAT observations, compute synthetic emission and polarization maps, and assess detectability with SKAO to distinguish between competing physical mechanisms.
AI.motivation: MeerKAT observations have revealed an unexpected and growing population of thin, highly collimated synchrotron threads in radio galaxies (filaments, rings, ribbons) whose physical origin and stability remain poorly understood despite their ubiquity.
AI.method: Three-dimensional, two-temperature general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic (GRMHD) simulations of realistically launched jets from supermassive black holes, with synthetic synchrotron emission and polarization maps computed from the simulations.
AI.result: Predictions of morphology, brightness profiles, and polarization patterns for collimated synchrotron threads, and assessment of their detectability with SKAO.
AI.conclusion: Upcoming SKA observations can distinguish between competing physical models (shock compression, magnetic flux tube formation, reconnection-driven filaments) and illuminate the magnetic origin of the collimated synchrotron threads observed by MeerKAT.

title: Unraveling the Imprints of Fluctuation-dynamo on the Intracluster Medium with the SKA
comment: PublishedinAdvancingAstrophysicswiththeSKAII(AASKAII),2026(arXiv:2606.20366). Report-no:AASKAII/AritraBasu01
summary: Studying the morphology and coherence scale of the magnetic fields in synchrotron emitting halos of galaxy clusters through detection of polarized synchrotron emission is important in order to understand how they distribute relativistic plasma, their contribution to pressure balance, and how they may affect gas content in galaxies and set up initial conditions during non-linear collapse to eventually form galaxies in the intracluster medium (ICM). Using synthetic maps over broad-bandwidths, generated from high resolution magnetohydrodynamic simulations of fluctuation dynamo, we study the efficacy of SKA-Low and Mid in Array Assembly AA4 in our quest for detecting polarized synchrotron emission from the intracluster medium (ICM). Fluctuation dynamo action in the ICM are expected to generate ubiquitous filamentary and sheet-like magnetic field structures. The associated synchrotron emission projected in the plane of the sky appear highly filamentary that can span hundreds of kiloparsecs. Such filaments can be robustly identified and quantified through high angular resolution ($\lesssim 1^{\prime\prime}$), sensitive observations (about $\rm 0.25\textrm{--}1\,μJy\,beam^{-1}$) above about 3\,GHz, a niche for the SKA-Mid in Band\,5a. Statistical properties of polarized emission and morphological measures, such as, Minkowski functionals, can then be used to infer the turbulence driving scales in the ICM with deep observations of galaxy clusters using SKA-Mid. Availability of a Band\,4 receiver covering 2--4\,GHz would be a major boost in studying the polarization properties of the ICM.

AI.tldr: Using MHD simulations of fluctuation dynamo, this paper demonstrates that SKA-Mid (Band 5a) can detect polarized synchrotron emission from filamentary magnetic fields in the ICM, and that Minkowski functionals can infer turbulence driving scales, with a Band 4 receiver (2–4 GHz) significantly boosting polarization studies.
AI.motivation: To understand the morphology, coherence scale, and pressure balance of magnetic fields in galaxy cluster halos via polarized synchrotron emission, and to assess how these fields distribute relativistic plasma and affect gas content in galaxies and ICM.
AI.method: Synthetic broad-bandwidth maps generated from high-resolution MHD simulations of fluctuation dynamo were used to evaluate the detection capabilities of SKA-Low and SKA-Mid (AA4) for polarized synchrotron emission from the ICM.
AI.result: Filamentary and sheet-like magnetic structures spanning hundreds of kiloparsecs can be robustly identified with high angular resolution (≲1″), sensitive observations (~0.25–1 μJy beam⁻¹) above ~3 GHz (SKA-Mid Band 5a). Minkowski functionals enable statistical inference of turbulence driving scales.
AI.conclusion: SKA-Mid is well-suited for detecting polarized ICM emission; adding a Band 4 receiver (2–4 GHz) would greatly enhance polarization studies of galaxy clusters.

title: Extreme Mass Ratio Inspirals in Light of Quasi-periodic Eruptions: Milli-Hertz Gravitational Wave Background
comment: 9 pages, 2 figures, and comments are welcome!
summary: Quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) are repeated X-ray bursts originating in galactic nuclei. Of the many proposed models, the favored model is the disk-collision model in which a stellar mass orbiter collides with a disk formed from a tidal disruption event, generating flares twice per orbit. In this model QPEs are tracers of circular extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs) and can be used to infer the EMRI formation rate and estimate their contribution to the stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) in the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) band. Whether the secondary is a stellar-mass black hole or a main sequence star is still debated and leads to different results for the EMRI rate and SGWB. We obtain fiducial rates -- subject to systematic uncertainties -- of $R_{\rm SE} = 2.88\times10^{-6}$ per galaxy per year for stellar EMRIs and $R_{\rm BHE} = 6.07\times10^{-6}$ per galaxy per year for black hole EMRIs, then estimate their contribution to the SGWB. We find that only black hole EMRIs contribute to the 1 - 10 milliHertz band resolvable by LISA, and depending on the secondary mass and formation radius can contribute from just below the LISA sensitivity curve to roughly two orders of magnitude above it. Stellar EMRIs, being tidally disrupted before reaching the 1 - 10 milliHertz band, only contribute to sub-milliHertz frequencies and remain below the LISA sensitivity curve.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates the connection between quasi-periodic eruptions (QPEs) and extreme mass ratio inspirals (EMRIs), finding that black hole EMRIs can contribute significantly (up to ~100× above LISA sensitivity) to the stochastic gravitational wave background in the 1-10 mHz band, while stellar EMRIs are tidally disrupted and remain below detectability.
AI.motivation: To use QPEs as tracers for inferring EMRI formation rates and estimating their contribution to the stochastic gravitational wave background (SGWB) in the LISA band, given that the disk-collision model for QPEs involves an orbiter striking a TDE disk twice per orbit.
AI.method: The authors compute fiducial EMRI rates under two scenarios (stellar-mass black hole secondary vs. main sequence star secondary), derive rates per galaxy per year, and estimate the resulting SGWB in the LISA frequency band.
AI.result: Stellar EMRIs: R_SE = 2.88×10⁻⁶ per galaxy per year; Black hole EMRIs: R_BHE = 6.07×10⁻⁶ per galaxy per year. Only black hole EMRIs contribute to the 1-10 mHz LISA band, potentially exceeding LISA sensitivity by up to ~100×. Stellar EMRIs are tidally disrupted before reaching this band and remain sub-threshold.
AI.conclusion: The nature of the secondary (BH vs. star) critically affects both the EMRI rate and SGWB detectability; black hole secondaries can produce a detectable signal in LISA, while stellar secondaries cannot.

title: An ACA map of a molecular cloud interacting with supernova remnant W28
comment: 22 pages, 9 figures, 5 tables, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Supernova remnants (SNRs) strongly influence the physical and chemical properties of the molecular clouds (MCs) with which they interact. We carried out a high-resolution observation toward W28F, a chemically rich MC interacting with SNR W28, with the Atacama Compact Array (ACA) in Band 7. Significant emission (> 10 sigma) of CO, CH3OH, p-H2CO, SiO and SO is detected. We reveal the clumpy structures of the shocked MC, with different spatial distributions between CH3OH and SiO. We select six molecular clumps to conduct spectral decomposition and non-local-thermodynamic-equilibrium analysis with the CH3OH and p-H2CO lines. The best-fit results show a H2 density of nH2 ~ (1-3) * 10^5 cm^-3 and a gas temperature of Tgas ~ 50-170 K in most of the fitted components. The H2 density and gas temperature show a clear anti-correlation across different regions, with the thermal pressure consistent with that of the adjacent X-ray-emitting hot plasma. This is consistent with the picture that the SNR shocks propagate into multi-phase gas, with a pressure balance existing between different phases. We propose that the high abundance ratio between E-CH3OHand A-CH3OH (> 0.9) suggests extra gas-phase processes to enhance this ratio, such as proton exchange with H3+ and HCO+. The chemical segregation between CH3OH and SiO, in both the spatial and spectral regime, can be explained by the fact that CH3OH traces slow shocks while SiO traces fast shocks.

AI.tldr: High-resolution ACA Band 7 observations of the shocked molecular cloud W28F (interacting with SNR W28) reveal clumpy structures, multi-phase gas with pressure balance, and chemical segregation between CH3OH (slow shocks) and SiO (fast shocks), with an anti-correlation between H2 density and gas temperature.
AI.motivation: To understand how supernova remnants physically and chemically influence the molecular clouds they interact with, using high-resolution observations of the chemically rich cloud W28F.
AI.method: ACA Band 7 observations; detection of CO, CH3OH, p-H2CO, SiO, SO lines; spectral decomposition and non-LTE analysis using CH3OH and p-H2CO lines across six selected clumps.
AI.result: H2 density nH2 ~ (1-3)×10^5 cm^-3 and gas temperature Tgas ~ 50-170 K; anti-correlation between density and temperature; thermal pressure consistent with adjacent X-ray hot plasma; E-CH3OH/A-CH3OH abundance ratio > 0.9; spatial/spectral segregation between CH3OH and SiO.
AI.conclusion: SNR shocks propagate into multi-phase gas with pressure balance; the high E/A methanol ratio suggests extra gas-phase processes (proton exchange with H3+, HCO+); CH3OH and SiO trace slow and fast shocks respectively, explaining their chemical segregation.

title: A Model for Magnetic Reconnection as the Origin of TeV Outbursts from NGC 1275
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, accepted for publication in PRD
summary: NGC 1275 showed two TeV $γ$-ray outbursts between November 2022 and January 2023, as detected by the Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory (LHAASO). The source was also active in the X-ray and GeV bands during the TeV outburst period. Very-long-baseline radio observations reported a sudden acceleration and deflection of a jet knot in late 2022, before the main TeV activity. Motivated by this sequence, we examine whether magnetic reconnection triggered by the interaction between the jet and the ambient medium can explain the TeV flares. In this picture, reconnection produces many plasmoids, and a large ``monster'' plasmoid becomes the main flare region. We model the low-state emission with a multi-zone stochastic-dissipation component and add a compact reconnection-powered region for the flaring state. We then compare leptonic and hadronic interpretations. The leptonic model explains the enhanced X-ray emission as electron synchrotron radiation and the TeV emission mainly as inverse-Compton radiation. A pure proton--proton model can also produce TeV photons if dense target gas is present, but it requires a compact cloud with a density above the values directly inferred from free--free absorption and a large proton power. These requirements are demanding, but they do not by themselves exclude the hadronic interpretation, because the gas may be compressed by the jet or may contain denser cloud cores. Our results show that magnetic reconnection in the parsec-scale jet is a viable origin of the 2022--2023 TeV activity of NGC 1275, while better constraints on the gas density and jet power are needed to distinguish between leptonic and hadronic radiation channels.

AI.tldr: NGC 1275 exhibited TeV γ-ray outbursts detected by LHAASO (2022-2023). We propose magnetic reconnection triggered by jet-ambient interaction as the origin. A leptonic model (synchrotron + inverse-Compton) explains multi-wavelength data well, while a hadronic model requires extreme gas densities and jet power. Reconnection in the parsec-scale jet is a viable mechanism, but distinguishing channels needs better constraints.
AI.motivation: To explain the TeV γ-ray outbursts of NGC 1275 observed by LHAASO between November 2022 and January 2023, motivated by the preceding jet knot acceleration/deflection detected by VLBI radio observations in late 2022.
AI.method: Model the low-state emission using a multi-zone stochastic-dissipation component and add a compact reconnection-powered region for flaring. Compare leptonic (synchrotron + inverse-Compton) and hadronic (proton-proton) interpretations.
AI.result: The leptonic model naturally explains enhanced X-ray (synchrotron) and TeV (inverse-Compton) emission. The hadronic model can work but requires a compact cloud with gas density exceeding free-free absorption constraints and large proton power, which is demanding but not ruled out.
AI.conclusion: Magnetic reconnection in the parsec-scale jet is a viable origin for NGC 1275's TeV activity, but better constraints on gas density and jet power are needed to distinguish between leptonic and hadronic channels.

title: MSA-3D: Rotation Curves and Dark Matter Fractions at z~0.5-1.7 with JWST/NIRSpec
comment: 21 pages + 8 appendix + 15 supplementary material, 14 figures, submitted to A&A
summary: We present rotation curves and inner mass distributions for 30 star-forming galaxies at $0.5<z<1.7$, observed with JWST/NIRSpec as part of the MSA-3D Cycle 1 survey. Combining spatially resolved ionised-gas kinematics with JWST/NIRCam imaging, we constrain baryonic and dark matter contributions through forward dynamical modelling for galaxies extending down to stellar masses of $\sim10^{9}M_\odot$. For the 23 galaxies in our primary statistical sample, we find predominantly rotationally supported disks with intrinsic dispersions $σ_0\sim31$-65 km s$^{-1}$ and a wide range of dark matter fractions, $f_{DM}(R_e)\sim0.1$-0.9, with a median of 0.63 and substantial galaxy-to-galaxy scatter of $\sim0.2$ dex. These results are supported by a complementary consistency check using stellar mass maps and SFR-derived gas profiles. Among the 19 galaxies reaching $\gtrsim2R_e$, we identify six rising, six flat, and seven falling rotation curves. These classes define an observed ordering from rotationally dominated, dark-matter-rich disks ($V_{rot}/σ_0\approx4$, $f_{DM}\gtrsim0.7$) to more dispersion-supported systems with centrally concentrated baryonic mass distributions ($V_{rot}/σ_0\approx2$, $f_{DM}\lesssim0.55$). The stellar Tully-Fisher relation lies close to the local relation evolved under the adopted self-similar $Λ$CDM scaling. A simplified seeing-degradation test shifts the inferred normalisation by ~0.2 dex at fixed $V_c$, suggesting that spatial resolution contributes to, but does not fully explain, differences among high-redshift Tully-Fisher measurements. Overall, MSA-3D provides a high-resolution extension of previous surveys toward lower stellar masses, spanning $9.0 < \log(M_\star/M_\odot) < 11.2$, and reinforces that star-forming disks near $z\sim1$ span a broad range of dynamical states and inner mass distributions.

AI.tldr: JWST/NIRSpec MSA-3D survey reveals that 23 star-forming galaxies at z~0.5-1.7 are predominantly rotationally supported disks with high dark matter fractions (median f_DM(Re)=0.63), broad dynamical diversity, and a stellar Tully-Fisher relation consistent with local ΛCDM expectations.
AI.motivation: To extend dynamical studies of star-forming galaxies at high redshift toward lower stellar masses (~10^9 Msun) using JWST's high spatial resolution, and to constrain baryonic vs. dark matter contributions in the inner regions of galaxies at z~1.
AI.method: Forward dynamical modeling combining spatially resolved ionized-gas kinematics from JWST/NIRSpec (MSA-3D survey) with JWST/NIRCam imaging. Complementary consistency checks using stellar mass maps and SFR-derived gas profiles. Tully-Fisher relation analysis with seeing-degradation tests.
AI.result: 23 galaxies show rotationally supported disks (σ0 ~31-65 km/s), broad DM fraction range f_DM(Re)=0.1-0.9 (median 0.63, scatter ~0.2 dex). Six rising, six flat, seven falling rotation curves among 19 galaxies. Stellar Tully-Fisher relation close to local ΛCDM scaling; seeing-degradation shifts normalization by ~0.2 dex.
AI.conclusion: Star-forming disks at z~1 span a broad range of dynamical states and inner mass distributions, with MSA-3D providing high-resolution extension to lower stellar masses (log M*/Msun = 9.0-11.2). Spatial resolution contributes to but does not fully explain differences among high-z Tully-Fisher measurements.

title: Fe Kα equivalent-width mapping with 3D radiative transfer calculation: A general model and application to the RS Canum Venaticorum-type stars with XRISM/Resolve
comment: 12 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication in Publications of the Astronomical Society of Japan
summary: The Fe K $α$ fluorescence line at 6.4 keV has long been used to probe the relative geometry between photoionizing X-ray sources and surrounding cold material in a wide range of astrophysical systems. With the advent of the X-ray microcalorimeter XRISM/Resolve, Fe K $α$ lines with equivalent widths down to $\sim 5$ eV-previously inaccessible-are now detectable, and even non-detections can place upper limits of a few eV, making non-detections themselves valuable for constraining the geometry. Considering that Fe K $α$-based geometric diagnostics are entering a new stage in the microcalorimeter era, we present Fe K $α$ equivalent-width maps computed with the three-dimensional Monte Carlo radiative-transfer code SKIRT for a generalized configuration consisting of a spherical reflector of radius $R_{*}$ and a point source located at a height $h$ above the surface. The equivalent-width maps exhibit two characteristic features: (1) an increase toward the center of the projected surface of the sphere; and (2) an overall decrease with increasing $h/R_{*}$. The key point is that we confirm these features for equivalent widths of $< 40$ eV, a regime that has become accessible for the first time thanks to the improved detection threshold from $\sim 50$ eV with Chandra/HETG to $\sim 5$ eV with XRISM/Resolve. As an illustrative application, we compare the maps with XRISM/Resolve spectra of three RS Canum Venaticorum-type stars (GT Muscae, $σ$ Geminorum, and HR 1099) and constrain the locations of the flare loop and coronal bright points in these systems. Because the maps are constructed for a highly generalized point-source--spherical-reflector geometry, they are readily applicable to many other objects, including X-ray binaries and cataclysmic variables.

AI.tldr: This paper presents 3D Monte Carlo radiative-transfer simulations of Fe Kα equivalent-width maps for a point source above a spherical reflector, showing two key features: central EW increase and overall decrease with height. The maps, validated for EWs < 40 eV, are applied to XRISM/Resolve spectra of three RS CVn stars to constrain flare loop and coronal bright point locations.
AI.motivation: With XRISM/Resolve's improved detection threshold (~5 eV) over Chandra/HETG (~50 eV), Fe Kα lines with small equivalent widths are now detectable, and non-detections can place meaningful upper limits. This enables new geometric diagnostics of X-ray sources and surrounding cold material, requiring updated theoretical maps for the microcalorimeter era.
